# Load the Data

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
install.packages("broom")
install.packages("knitr")
library(broom)
library(knitr)

movies <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2021/2021-03-09/movies.csv',
                          na = c("", "NA", "#N/A", "N/A"))
glimpse(movies)

# 1794 observations, 34 variables
```

# Section 1: Linear Regression
Research Question: Among these movies, how does domestic gross revenue change with budget? Is that pattern different for movies that pass vs. fail the Bechdel test?

    # Part A:
Budget_2013 has 0 missing values. Domgross_2013 has 18 missing values.

```{r}
# Summary of Budget variable
summary(movies$budget_2013)
# mean = 55,464,608, median = 36,995,786
# mean is very far from median, let's check the distribution in a histogram and boxplot
ggplot(movies, aes(x = budget_2013)) + geom_histogram() 
ggplot(movies, aes(x = budget_2013)) + geom_boxplot()
# The distribution is skewed heavily to the right, shown by both the histogram and the boxplot. The boxplot is showing lots and lots of outliers.
```

```{r}
# Summary of Domestic Gross Revenue variable
summary(movies$domgross_2013)
# mean = 9.517e+07, median = 5.599e+07
# again, mean far from median. Highest grossing/budgeted movies must be skewing the distribution quite a bit
ggplot(movies, aes(x = domgross_2013)) + geom_histogram() 
ggplot(movies, aes(x = domgross_2013)) + geom_boxplot()
# skewed to the right, lots of outliers 
```

```{r}
# Quick look at Bechdel Test variable
# 0 missing values
table(movies$binary) 
# 803 pass, 991 fail
table(movies$clean_test)
```

```{r}
# Try log-transforming the budget2013 and domgross2013 data to see if it's easier to see before we have to cut out super high outliers.
ggplot(movies, aes(x = log10(budget_2013))) + geom_histogram()
ggplot(movies, aes(x = log10(domgross_2013))) + geom_histogram()
# These look a little better, but I might get rid of some of the highest values along with the NAs, because they exhibit too much leverage anyway. 
```

Cleaning the Data: remove NAs and extreme values 

```{r}
# Removing NAs from domgross_2013
cleanrev_budget2013 <- movies %>% 
    filter(!is.na(domgross_2013), domgross_2013 < 5e+08) %>%
    filter(budget_2013 < 2.5e+08) %>%
    select(domgross_2013, budget_2013, binary)
summary(cleanrev_budget2013)
ggplot(cleanrev_budget2013, aes(x = domgross_2013)) + geom_boxplot()
ggplot(cleanrev_budget2013, aes(x = budget_2013)) + geom_boxplot()

# Looks a little better, going to proceed with this for now, looking at movies with a domestic gross revenue under 500 million dollars and budget under 250 million dollars. Hopefully this will result in the models fitting a little better with less extreme values that may cause it to overfit these really expensive values. And we want to get a general picture of the relationship between budget and revenue, not predicting whether a super high budget will produce a really high revenue.

```

Now that data is cleaned, let's make a model.

```{r}
# Linear regression model of the relationship between budget_2013 and domgross_2013, including the interaction of Bechdel test status (binary). 
linear_regression_model <- lm(domgross_2013 ~ budget_2013 * binary,
                            data = cleanrev_budget2013)
summary(linear_regression_model)
dev.off()
plot(linear_regression_model)

# Diagnostic plots are concerning, I think the outliers are really affecting the model. I will try and redo the model with data that excludes the positive outliers.
```

Cleaning data again: excluding values greater than Q3 + 1.5*IQR for both variables 

```{r}
#outlier threshold for budget_2013
summary(movies$budget_2013)
78337905 + 1.5*(78337905 - 16068918) #171741386
summary(movies$domgross_2013)
1.217e+08 + 1.5*(1.217e+08 - 2.055e+07) #273425000

# clean the data again now, keeping data below these values
cleanrev_budget2013 <- movies %>% 
    filter(!is.na(domgross_2013), domgross_2013 < 273425000) %>%
    filter(budget_2013 < 171741386) %>%
    select(domgross_2013, budget_2013, binary)

summary(cleanrev_budget2013)
ggplot(cleanrev_budget2013, aes(x = domgross_2013)) + geom_histogram()
ggplot(cleanrev_budget2013, aes(x = budget_2013)) + geom_histogram()
# Distributions are still not normal. But going to make a model from this new cleaned data and then check assumptions.

new_linear_regression <- lm(domgross_2013 ~ budget_2013 * binary,
                            data = cleanrev_budget2013)
summary(new_linear_regression)
ggplot(cleanrev_budget2013, 
        aes( x = budget_2013, y = domgross_2013, color = binary)) +
        geom_point() +
        geom_smooth(method = "lm")

```

Part B: Interpretation
1) The coefficient for budget, as a description of the movies is 0.8134
2) The coefficient for the interaction term is 0.0696, which is also the difference in the fitted lines between PASS/FAIL the Bechdel test. This means the model suggests that the slope for movies that pass the Bechdel test is 0.0696 higher than those that fail. 
3) The model predicts that there is a $66,960 difference in the rate of change of domestic gross revenue between movies based on whether they pass or fail the Bechdel test. The p-value associated with the interaction of Bechdel test status is 0.326, which is not sufficient evidence to suggest that we reject the hypothesis that Bechdel test status has a significant interaction on budget and its relationship to domestic gross revenue. The p-value associated with the relationship between budget and gross revenue is very small, suggesting it could be significant, but we need to check the assumptions to make sure it is a valid model.

Part C: Diagnostic Plots

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(new_linear_regression)

```

Normality: Looking at the Q-Q Residual plot, we can see that a large amount of the points fall off of the line, giving reason to suggest that there is not normality. 
Constant Variance: The Residuals vs. Fitted Plot shows what looks like it could be a random scatter around 0, though with lower fitted values the residuals are definitely more tightly clustered around 0, while in higher fitted values they are a bit more spread out. This could also have to do just with the higher number of smaller values in the dataset.
Influential Points: There are a lot of points with really high leverage, which was a concern I had from the beginning.

I don't think the model assumptions are reasonably met for this comparison. A different type of model might be needed or even more of the extreme values need to be excluded from the dataset for analysis. I also don't think the fitted lines separating the data into PASS/FAIL are good representations of the data. The data is super scattered and the lines imply a much stronger relationship than I think our model summary showed us.
